questions.question: A design uses a 32‑bit DSP processor and an ASIC for signal processing. According to the generation‑based classification, to which generation does this design belong?
questions.explanation:
Third Generation embedded systems are characterized by the use of powerful 32‑bit processors, 16‑bit microcontrollers, DSPs, and ASICs. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: An embedded product is built around a single System‑on‑Chip (SoC) that integrates CPU, memory, and peripherals. Which generation does this product represent?
questions.explanation:
The advent of System‑on‑Chip (SoC) defines the Fourth Generation of embedded systems. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: Which processing core type is most closely associated with the Third Generation of embedded systems?

options.D: Pure hardware logic without programmable cores

questions.explanation:
Third Generation designs commonly incorporate ASICs and DSPs as processing cores. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: Compared to Third Generation embedded systems, Fourth Generation systems primarily differ in that they:

options.B: Replace separate processor and peripheral chips with an integrated SoC.
options.C: Eliminate the need for any software.

questions.explanation:
Fourth Generation introduces SoC integration, consolidating processing and peripherals that were separate in the Third Generation. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: A designer selects a 16‑bit microcontroller together with a DSP for a new industrial controller. Which generation classification best fits this design?
questions.explanation:
The combination of 16‑bit microcontrollers and DSPs is a hallmark of Third Generation embedded systems. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: Which of the following devices is most likely an example of a Fourth Generation embedded system?

options.A: A thermostat using a simple 8‑bit microcontroller.
options.B: A handheld calculator with discrete CPU and memory chips.
options.C: A wearable fitness tracker built on a single SoC.
options.D: A legacy vending machine using a fixed‑function ASIC.

questions.explanation:
Wearable devices built on a single SoC reflect the SoC‑centric Fourth Generation. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: In generation‑based classification, which generation typically still employs separate processor and peripheral components rather than a unified SoC?
questions.explanation:
Third Generation systems use powerful processors and separate peripheral chips; SoC integration arrives in the Fourth Generation. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: The transition from Third to Fourth Generation embedded systems is primarily driven by:

options.A: The need for larger physical board size.
options.B: The development of integrated System‑on‑Chip technology.
options.C: A shift back to analog circuitry.
options.D: The removal of any programmable cores.

questions.explanation:
The key driver for Fourth Generation is the advent of SoC technology that integrates multiple functions onto a single chip. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects the evolution of processing cores across generations?

options.A: First Generation used SoC, Third Generation reverted to discrete chips.
options.B: Second Generation introduced ASICs, Fourth Generation eliminated them.
options.C: Third Generation emphasized powerful 32‑bit processors and DSPs; Fourth Generation moved to SoC integration.

questions.explanation:
The progression described matches the context: Third Generation with 32‑bit/DSP/ASIC, Fourth Generation with SoC. [Page 22]

---

questions.question: Arrange the following generations in chronological order from earliest to latest: (i) SoC‑based systems, (ii) Systems using 32‑bit processors and DSPs, (iii) Systems based on simple 8‑bit microcontrollers.
questions.explanation: Early embedded systems started with simple 8‑bit microcontrollers, then progressed to 32‑bit/DSP/ASIC (Third Generation), and finally to SoC (Fourth Generation). [Page 22]
